title: Theme or Topic?
summary: Three clusters of coded extracts from an invented dataset, each with four candidate statements. The learner sorts every candidate into topic summary, useful staging post, developed theme, or beyond what the data can carry, and receives a written note on all four. The three over-reaching candidates fail in three different ways: one asserts a cause, one attributes intent to an institution nobody interviewed, and one imports a construct together with a between-person comparison. A second challenge asks which rewrites would give a weak section a central organising concept.
learningObjectives: Distinguish a topic summary from a developed theme in reflexive thematic analysis.
Name the central organising concept a candidate theme is built around.
Recognise a descriptive statement that is a legitimate stage in an analysis but not yet a theme.
Identify claims that go beyond what interview data can support, and say why in each case.
Rewrite a topic heading so that it carries an analytic claim.
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; everything runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Native selects, checkboxes and buttons, each with an explicit label and grouped in a fieldset with a legend. There are no charts: every output is text, so no visual-only information exists to be paired. The cluster - its name, its codes and two short quotations - is pinned to the top of the stage so the material being judged stays visible while the four candidates below are classified. Each feedback block prints both the learner's classification and the tool's in words, so the coloured left border is a redundant cue, and each candidate control carries a visible 'Candidate A' tag as well as its position. The stage track marks the current and checked clusters with visually hidden text as well as styling. Changes announce full sentences through the polite live region, focus moves to the challenge heading when it opens, forced-colours rules are provided, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
readmeTopic: Topic summary, staging post, developed theme, or a claim the data cannot carry
simulationNotes: Three clusters of codes and short quotations drawn from the same six invented interview extracts used by the Thematic Analysis Coding Laboratory and the Reflexivity and Alternative Theme Builder in this module, so the three tools run as a sequence. Each cluster has four candidate statements, one in each category. The four categories are a teaching simplification: real candidate themes sit on a continuum and several of these could be argued into a neighbouring category. The developed theme offered for each cluster is defensible rather than uniquely correct, and the second challenge makes that explicit by accepting two different themes for the same extracts. The three over-reaching candidates are constructed to fail in three distinct ways so that over-claiming is not reduced to a single habit. No participant, interview, institution or study is represented.
